full_judgment: 5. The only question remains is whether the amendments of the Articles of Association were done regularly or not. At the instance of the petitioner the minutes of the meeting of the shareholders of the company were called for to see whether such amendments were passed or not. The relevant minutes for this purpose is ext. 2 (ii) and Ext. 9 (ii). Ext. 2 (ii) is the copy filed with the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies whereas the Ext. 9 (ii) is the copy filed by the respondent No. 2. The minutes relate to a meeting held on the 15th October, 1962 which was apparently attended by the petitioner, respondent No. 2 and their mother. From the minutes it appears that various clauses of the Articles of Association were amended and altered although the nature of the amendments or alterations were not specified. The meeting was apparently held under the Chairmanship of the petitioner and the petitioner's signature at the bottom of the minutes is also appearing. The signature has been admitted by the petitioner himself to be his own signature, but in his evidence he denied to have participated in any such meeting where the amendments and alterations of the Articles of Association were made. According to the petitioner, though his signature was obtained in the copies of the minutes but such signature was obtained from him earlier at the bottom of certain blank white papers which were surreptitiously used for the purpose of alleged fraudulent amendments and alterations of the Articles of Association of the company. So far as the copies of the minutes are concerned, it is very difficult to reject these copies as these are available from the office of the Registrar of the Joint Stock Companies. Even if it is assumed that the petitioner had signed certain blank papers and these were used for the purpose of amendments and alterations of the Articles of Association, but on the face of these papers, it is not possible to come to any such definite finding that such fraud was actually practiced upon the petitioner. It only proves an imprudent action on the part of the petitioner showing his lack of common sense in dealing with the affairs of the management of the company. Although brothers might have familiar family relationship as such, but such smooth relationship cannot be the basis of any presumption, while managing the affairs of any company. No specific remedy in this regard is available in this proceeding under section 162 of the Companies Act, while considering the legality or the propriety for making any order for winding up of any company.
